title: The Wire Only Tells Once
passages:
Wren knelt on the wet deck planks and set the twin spool down between her and Sol. Two reels side by side, one for the descent wire and one for its slack. She threaded the leader through the reader, the box that plays back a diver's recorded wire, clicked the pinch roller shut, and spun the take-up reel by hand. The wire sang a soft, even note as it moved through the head.

"Here," Wren said. She kept her eyes on the reels, not on Sol. "Eleven seconds. Snipped clean. The shears are in my pocket. My hand did it."

Sol stood at the rail, one hand on the bell frame, watching the Kettle's gate where Quill waited with the berth book. The storm bell had started its count, a slow brass toll that shook the Marrow's timbers. Dey lay on the deck mat behind them, gray around the mouth, rattling with every breath.

"Show me," Sol said.

Wren fed the wire forward. The reader clicked. A span passed the head, then stopped on a clean cut, both ends blunt and shiny, no fray. Eleven seconds of nothing between them. She stopped the reel.

"Fifty-two minutes," Wren said. "That's what the cut was built to hide. I don't remember any of it. Not the descent, not the can going over the side, not why I'd cut my own wire."

The spit can was the hard-shell drop-box a diver jettisons so the crew gets their record if they don't surface. Its beacon was still transmitting at forty-two meters on six hours of battery. Wren had found it missing from her harness clip earlier, still pinging from depth.

Sol didn't move from the rail. Her face was calm, which was worse than shouting. "The rule on this boat is slates run, nobody cuts, nobody goes down alone."

"I know," Wren said. "I broke all three."

"You went down alone."

"I don't remember going down at all."

"That doesn't make it better." Sol stepped closer, her boots loud on the wet planks. "Hand me the shears."

Wren pulled them from her pocket and dropped them into Sol's palm. Sol closed her fingers around them. They were heavy, rust-spotted at the joint, the kind of tool that could cut a diver's line or a wire span with one squeeze. Eleven seconds of nothing sat on the reader between two clean cuts, and Sol's fist was closed around the shears.

Sol turned the shears over in her palm. The blades caught the gray light coming through the Kettle's gate. She didn't speak.

"Say it," Sol said at last.

Wren wiped her hands on her trousers, leaving a smear of wire grease. "The wire only tells once. You cut a span out, that stretch of record is gone for good. No backup, no second copy, nothing to patch it with. You play a span through the reader, it runs from the master spool onto the take-up reel and it's spent. You can't rewind it, you can't run it back, and you can't thread the same length twice. The record tells its story one time, and then it's silent."

She pointed at the master spool, the larger reel on the left side of the twin spool, where the full descent wire lay wound in overlapping loops. "There's one snipped length still on the master. A second cut. I found it when I wound the wire back after your last run. I haven't threaded it. I haven't dared."

Sol didn't lower her hand. "How long?"

"Eleven seconds. Or less. It's a blind span—no leader, no slack on the take-up side, just wire between two fresh cuts. My cuts. I made them and then I left them sitting there."

"That's not eleven seconds of nothing," Sol said. "That's eleven seconds of something you don't want to hear."

"I don't know what's on it."

"You know well enough."

Dey coughed from the mat, a wet, racking sound that shook his shoulders. He didn't open his eyes. "Get on with it," he muttered. "Before the bell drowns us all."

Wren kicked his boot, light but sharp. "Sleep it off, diver. You're not the one holding the shears."

Dey made a noise that might have been a laugh. "Cut it already. Whatever she did, it's already done."

Sol looked at Wren, not at the wire. "You're afraid of your own record."

"I'm afraid of what happens after I play it," Wren said. "Once it's spent, it's gone. That's the rule. I cut it, so it's mine to play—or not."

Sol's fingers tightened on the shears until the rust-spotted joint creaked. "Then play it."

"I haven't decided if I want to hear my own voice tell me what I did."

Outside, the storm bell tolled again, low and slow, shaking the Marrow's timbers. The reader clicked as the take-up reel settled, a small mechanical sound in the quiet. The unplayed span waited on the master, eleven seconds of wire that had been cut out of Wren's own record, still unspent, still unheard, and still hers.
